strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in visual generation: composing heterogeneous sources of knowledge at inference time, including image/video generative models, VLM-based rewards, graphics engines, and physics simulators.

The Product-of-Experts framing is appealing and gives a unified language for several useful control settings, such as object insertion, physics-conditioned video generation, and regional text-to-image composition.
The method is training-free and modular, which is practically attractive because it can reuse strong pretrained backbones and external simulators without collecting aligned training data.

The experiments cover multiple generation scenarios and include several relevant baselines, ablations on conditional sampling and discriminative experts, and both qualitative and automatic quantitative metrics.
The visual examples suggest that the approach can improve controllability in cases where monolithic image/video generators fail to follow precise pose, depth, or motion constraints.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is somewhat incremental relative to prior work on compositional diffusion, product-of-experts generation, reward-guided diffusion, and SMC-based steering. The paper does not clearly isolate what is fundamentally new beyond combining these ingredients in several applications.

The sampling algorithm is only loosely justified as AIS/SMC. The transition kernels, resampling weights, final max-selection step, and use of approximate endpoint rewards do not establish that the procedure samples from the stated product distribution, so the probabilistic claims are stronger than the derivation supports.

The conditional sampling approximation in Eq. 7 is heuristic and insufficiently validated. It is unclear when matching flow vectors between regions corresponds to a meaningful conditional distribution, and the paper gives limited analysis of failure modes or incompatibility between experts.

The empirical evaluation is small: 30 image-editing scenes, 12 object-centric video scenes, 9 full-scene simulation scenes, and mostly qualitative text-to-image results. This is too limited to strongly support broad claims about visual generation or controllability.

Several metrics rely on GPT-4o or learned aesthetic/reward models, with no human study and no statistical significance testing. Many reported differences are small relative to the standard deviations, especially in video experiments.

Baselines are not always fully comparable. For image insertion, RF-Solver receives only coarse text rather than the graphics-engine control signal; for video, the initial frame is produced by the authors' own method, which can entangle stages; for text-to-image, there is no quantitative comparison to strong layout/control or compositional generation baselines.

The text-to-image regional composition section is underdeveloped: it shows a few examples but lacks benchmark-scale evaluation, failure analysis, and comparisons to established layout-to-image or attention-control methods.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details such as exact prompts for GPT-4o evaluation, LLM layout parsing prompts, hyperparameter selection, masks, reward scaling, random seeds, and code/model release status are either missing or deferred only partially to the appendix.

The computational cost is high relative to standard inference, with several minutes per sample on H200 GPUs and up to 30 minutes for the autoregressive setting, but the paper provides limited cost-quality tradeoff analysis.

The societal impact discussion is superficial given that the method explicitly improves controllable image and video synthesis, which could increase misuse risk for misinformation or targeted manipulation.

strengths: The paper targets an interesting and timely problem: composing heterogeneous sources of knowledge, including generative models, VLM rewards, graphics engines, and physics simulators, at inference time for controllable visual generation.
The product-of-experts framing is a reasonable high-level abstraction, and the paper connects it to AIS/SMC in a way that could be useful for organizing future systems.

The applications are visually compelling in places, especially graphics-engine-guided insertion and physics-guided video generation, and the method is tested across several task settings rather than only one narrow demo.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Product-of-experts composition, score/velocity composition, reward-guided diffusion, SMC guidance, regional diffusion composition, and simulator-conditioned video generation are all closely related to prior work. The paper mostly repackages these ingredients without clearly isolating a new algorithmic contribution.

The technical claims are substantially stronger than the method supports. The sampler is described as AIS/SMC for a product distribution, but the implementation uses many heuristics: deterministic flow steps, approximate Langevin steps, endpoint reward evaluation, median-threshold resampling, local masks, and final best-particle selection. This is not convincingly justified as sampling from the stated PoE distribution.

The conditional sampling derivation is weak. Equation (7) is an ad hoc compatibility penalty between predicted flows, and Appendix D.2 does not provide a convincing probabilistic derivation or evidence that it approximates the conditional expert distribution claimed in the main text.

The evaluation is too small and fragile for a top-tier conference. Image insertion uses only 30 scenes, object-centric video uses 12 scenes, full-scene video uses 9 scenes, and text-to-image regional composition appears to have only qualitative examples. These scales are insufficient to support broad claims about visual generation.

The baselines are incomplete and sometimes unfair. For image insertion, RF-Solver receives only a coarse text prompt rather than the same rich geometric controls. For regional text-to-image, important layout/regional diffusion and compositional generation baselines are missing. For video, comparisons to stronger simulator/depth/trajectory-conditioned systems are limited.

The metrics do not convincingly validate the claims. The paper relies heavily on GPT-4o automatic judging, aesthetic predictors, ImageReward, ViCLIP, and LPIPS to simulator renderings, but provides no human study, no confidence testing, and little discussion of metric reliability for these tasks.

Ablations are inadequate. The paper does not thoroughly isolate the effects of AIS vs simple score composition, MCMC step count, particle count, resampling strategy, reward expert choice, mask construction, compatibility weight, or compute budget. The claimed sample-efficiency benefits are therefore not well supported.

Reproducibility is weak. The project page is blank in the extracted manuscript, datasets and prompts are not fully specified, several hyperparameters are omitted or only partially reported, and the method depends on large proprietary or external models such as GPT-4o/o1-mini and H200-scale compute.

The method is computationally expensive, taking minutes per sample and up to 30 minutes in the autoregressive setting, but the paper does not give a careful quality/compute tradeoff or compare against simpler best-of-N or control-conditioned baselines under matched wall-clock budgets across all tasks.

The societal impact discussion is superficial given that the method explicitly improves controllable image/video generation, which can increase misuse risk for fabricated visual evidence. The paper acknowledges misinformation but offers no concrete mitigation or evaluation.

strengths: Clear and timely problem formulation: composing heterogeneous visual-generation knowledge sources at inference time is important, and the Product-of-Experts framing is natural and broadly applicable.

The method is appealingly training-free and flexible, combining generative backbones, VLM-style discriminative rewards, graphics-engine constraints, and physics-simulator inputs within one sampling framework.
Experiments cover several qualitatively distinct applications: graphics-guided object insertion, physics-guided video generation, and regional text-to-image composition.
Results are generally convincing at a high level, with consistent gains in controllability and text/semantic alignment over reasonable backbone-matched baselines.
The paper is well organized, with useful implementation details, ablations on conditional sampling and discriminative experts, and a candid discussion of compute and limitations.
weaknesses: The empirical scale is limited for a top-tier claim: 30 image-editing scenes, 12 object-centric video scenes, 9 full-scene simulation scenes, and mostly qualitative text-to-image examples leave uncertainty about robustness.

Several evaluations rely heavily on automatic VLM/GPT-4o judgments, with no human study and limited statistical testing; this is concerning because the method itself uses VLM rewards in some settings.

The sampling procedure is presented as PoE/AIS/SMC, but some practical components are approximate, such as velocity/score composition and the conditional sampling heuristic, with limited theoretical justification for correctness or bias in the final samples.

Baselines are somewhat narrow for each task, and some comparisons may favor the proposed method because it receives richer structured inputs or uses an edited initial frame produced by the authors' own pipeline.
Compute cost is high, especially for video generation, and the paper does not fully analyze the quality-compute tradeoff against simpler best-of-N or guidance approaches across all tasks.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript: many large proprietary or external components are involved, supplementary videos are referenced, and exact implementation/code availability is unclear.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: inference-time composition of heterogeneous visual generation constraints, including generative backbones, VLM rewards, graphics engines, and physics simulators.
The product-of-experts framing is conceptually clean and unifies several controllable image/video generation settings under one probabilistic view.
The proposed annealed MCMC plus SMC procedure is flexible and can use black-box discriminative rewards, which is practically attractive when gradients are unavailable or unreliable.

The paper demonstrates breadth across image insertion, physics-simulator-guided video generation, and layout-controlled text-to-image generation, with qualitative examples that make the intended use cases clear.
Ablations on conditional sampling and particle count provide some evidence that the main components improve controllability and alignment.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited relative to prior work on compositional diffusion/energy models, reward steering, annealed sampling, and SMC-based inference-time control. The paper mostly repackages known ingredients into a broad framework, with limited new theoretical insight.

The sampling procedure is not rigorously justified. Several steps are heuristic, especially the conditional sampling approximation in Eq. (6), the use of endpoint predictions for discriminator rewards, and the autoregressive case approximated by MAP-style gradient updates rather than the stated sampler.

The empirical evaluation is too small for the strength of the claims: 30 scenes for graphics-engine insertion, 12 scenes for object-centric video, 9 scenes for full-scene simulation, and 50 layout scenes. These sample sizes are not convincing for broad conclusions about fidelity, controllability, or generality.

Baselines are incomplete and sometimes not fully comparable. The paper does not consistently compare against strong task-specific editing, controllable video, reward-guided diffusion, or best-of-N/search baselines under matched compute.

Many metrics rely on GPT-4o, VQAScore, ImageReward, or other learned evaluators, some of which are also used as guidance/reward signals. This raises concerns about evaluator bias and circularity, and there is no human evaluation to validate perceptual claims.

Compute cost is high: several minutes per image/video sample and up to 25 minutes in layout experiments. The paper does not provide a careful quality-vs-compute comparison against simpler sampling or reranking alternatives.

The method appears sensitive to expert compatibility, regional masks, particle count, annealing schedule, reward scaling, and other implementation choices, but these sensitivities are not systematically studied.

Reproducibility is limited: important details such as hyperparameters, reward normalization, exact prompts, dataset construction, and failure cases are either sparse or deferred; no code or generated datasets are clearly promised.
The societal impact discussion is superficial given that the method explicitly improves controllable generation and object insertion, which could increase risks for deceptive media creation.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: inference-time composition of heterogeneous visual generation experts, including generative models, VLM rewards, graphics engines, and physics simulators.
The Product-of-Experts framing is conceptually clean and provides a unifying language for several controllable image/video generation settings.
The paper includes multiple application domains rather than a single narrow demo: object insertion, physics-guided video generation, and layout-controlled text-to-image generation.
Some ablations are useful, especially conditional sampling, particle count, and SMC resampling, and the qualitative examples suggest the approach can improve controllability in selected cases.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited relative to prior work on PoE/compositional diffusion, reward-guided sampling, AIS/SMC guidance, and inference-time model composition. The paper presents a broad framework, but many components appear to be known ideas combined with task-specific engineering.

The sampling methodology is not sufficiently justified. The claimed AIS/SMC framing is loose: the algorithm does not appear to provide correct AIS weighting, the final sample is selected by maximum reward rather than sampled from the target product distribution, and several kernels only approximately preserve the intended distributions.

Several key approximations are ad hoc, especially the conditional sampling update in Eq. (6) and the treatment of autoregressive experts via MAP-like gradient updates. These weaken the central claim of a principled probabilistic framework.

The evaluation is too small and fragile for the breadth of claims: 30 graphics-engine scenes, 12 object-centric video scenes, 9 full-scene video scenes, and 50 MIG-Bench scenes are not enough to establish robust generality.

The evaluation relies heavily on automatic metrics such as GPT-4o, VQAScore, ImageReward, and detector-based scores, without human studies or convincing validation that these metrics reflect the intended controllability and fidelity in these tasks.

The baseline comparisons are not fully convincing. Some baselines receive weaker or less structured inputs, some tasks use the authors' method to prepare inputs for all methods, and compute budgets are often mismatched or unclear.

The paper claims computational efficiency, but reported runtimes are high: minutes per image/video sample on H200 GPUs, up to 25 minutes for 32 particles and 30 minutes for autoregressive video. This undercuts the practical-efficiency claim.

The physics-simulator video evidence is particularly weak: datasets are tiny, metrics are indirect, and the qualitative results do not establish that the method reliably enforces physical correctness beyond tracking visual controls.

Reproducibility is limited. Many implementation details, hyperparameters, prompts, evaluation templates, datasets, and exact expert configurations are either deferred, underspecified, or dependent on proprietary models/evaluators.

The societal impact discussion is superficial given that the method explicitly improves fine-grained controllability of image and video generation, which can increase misuse risk for manipulation or misinformation.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and useful formulation of controllable visual generation as inference in a product-of-experts distribution over heterogeneous sources, including image/video generators, VLM rewards, graphics engines, and physics simulators.

The proposed annealed MCMC plus SMC sampling procedure is a sensible and practically motivated way to combine generative and discriminative experts without retraining, and the paper explains how it can be instantiated for flow-based and autoregressive models.

The applications are compelling: object insertion, physics-simulator-guided video generation, and layout/text-conditioned image generation demonstrate a flexible interface that goes beyond a single narrow benchmark.
Empirical results are generally positive across multiple tasks, with comparisons to relevant modern baselines and useful ablations on conditional sampling, particle count, and SMC resampling.

The work is timely and likely to be useful for researchers interested in inference-time composition, controllable generation, and integrating symbolic/simulator constraints with pretrained visual models.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than decisive: product-of-experts composition, annealed MCMC, SMC-based reward steering, and diffusion/model composition have substantial prior art, and the paper's main contribution is largely a practical synthesis and extension rather than a fundamentally new inference principle.

The theoretical grounding is somewhat thin. Several key implementation choices, especially the conditional sampling approximation and the use of endpoint predictions for discriminator rewards, are heuristic and not supported by strong analysis of bias, invariance, or convergence.

The empirical scale is limited for a top-tier claim: some evaluations use only 30, 12, or 9 scenes, and the text-to-image layout evaluation uses 50 samples from an 800-scene benchmark. This makes it hard to assess robustness across diverse prompts, assets, and failure modes.

Evaluation relies heavily on automatic metrics and GPT-4o/VLM judgments, with no human preference study despite the perceptual and controllability-focused nature of the claims. Statistical significance and variance across seeds are also not deeply analyzed.

The comparisons are not always fully satisfying: several baselines differ in available controls, backbone assumptions, or compute budget, and the method can be substantially more expensive than feedforward generation. Compute-quality tradeoffs are shown in one setting but not systematically across all tasks.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a complex system involving proprietary or large pretrained models, graphics/simulation pipelines, VLM evaluators, and many hyperparameters. It is not fully clear how easily others could reproduce the reported results.

The paper would benefit from a more candid and detailed failure analysis, especially for incompatible experts, mode collapse/particle degeneracy, cases where SMC does not help, and scenarios with more than a small number of experts.
